findings.text: When NewTimer, AfterFunc, or an initialized Timer's Reset computes a deadline, a zero or negative duration uses the current runtime clock reading. A positive duration is added to that reading. If the sum wraps to a negative value, the deadline is set to MaxInt64. These are deadline calculations; callback execution and channel delivery occur separately.

NewTimer allocates a channel with capacity 1, passes that channel and its pointer representation to newTimer, then assigns the same channel to the returned timer's C field. After returns the C field from its own NewTimer call. The NewTimer documentation promises synchronous, capacity-0 behavior as of Go 1.23. The runtime implementation that could reconcile the allocation with the public behavior is outside this excerpt.
findings.question: OPEN: How does the runtime make the capacity-1 allocation appear synchronous to callers, and under which runtime configurations does the capacity-0 guarantee apply?

findings.text: If the runtime defers sendTime after a channel timer's scheduled delivery, sendTime computes Now() minus the supplied delay and attempts a nonblocking send. If the channel can accept the value, that adjusted timestamp is delivered even when the receive happens much later. If the send cannot proceed, the default branch returns without delivering a value.
findings.question: OPEN: Should the promise to send the current time specify that deferred delivery carries a timestamp adjusted back toward the scheduled send time?

findings.text: For an AfterFunc timer with nil C, if Stop wins before expiration, it returns true and cancels the pending callback. A second Stop on the same timer, with no intervening Reset, returns false even though that callback never started. If expiration wins first, the timer dispatches f in its own goroutine and Stop returns false without waiting for f to finish.

citation.fragment: if t.Stop returns false, then the timer has already expired

findings.question: OPEN: Is the statement that f has started meant to apply only when expiration caused the false return, given that a previously successful Stop also makes a later Stop return false?

findings.text: If Reset runs while an AfterFunc timer is still active, it reschedules the pending callback on the same timer and returns true. If expiration has already dispatched the callback, Reset returns false and schedules another invocation on the same timer. The new invocation can overlap the first because Reset does not wait for it. Reset after a successful Stop also returns false and schedules an invocation, even if cancellation prevented the original invocation from starting.

citation.fragment: goroutine running f does not run concurrently with the prior

findings.text: Stop and Reset panic on a zero-value Timer. For a running NewTimer timer whose value has not been received, the Go 1.23 contract guarantees that either operation returns true. If the timer value is received first and the timer expires, the later operation returns false. Stop prevents a subsequent receive from getting a stale value, while Reset passes the existing timer to the runtime, keeps the same C channel, and prevents a subsequent receive from getting a value from the previous settings. A later Reset can make a receive succeed after an earlier Stop. The documented pre-Go-1.23 procedures use a drain after a false Stop or a stop-and-drain before Reset.

citation.fragment: any receive from t.C after Stop has returned is guaranteed to block

findings.question: OPEN: Should the post-Stop blocking guarantee explicitly cover only the interval before a later Reset can produce a new value?
